findings.description: Fallback to unverified TLS context when fetching package metadata from PyPI
findings.code_snippet:
def _request_context():
    yield None
    # fallback to non verified HTTPS (the information we request is not sensitive, so fallback)
    yield ssl._create_unverified_context()  # noqa: S323, SLF001
...
with urlopen(url, context=context) as file_handler:  # noqa: S310
findings.reasoning: _request_context() yields a verified context first, but on URLError it retries with ssl._create_unverified_context(). Any URLError (including a TLS certificate verification failure caused by a MITM) triggers the unverified retry, so an on-path attacker can serve forged PyPI JSON metadata. The data is used to pick the version of wheels to install (periodic update), so spoofed metadata can influence which packages are seeded into new environments. The code comment argues the data is not sensitive, but integrity is also at stake, not only confidentiality.

evidence.code_context: _request_context yields None (verified) then ssl._create_unverified_context(); _pypi_get_distribution_info loops over contexts and calls urlopen(url, context=context) for https://pypi.org/pypi/{distribution}/json, breaking only on success.
evidence.dataflow_analysis: Not traced with the tool. The fallback is structural: the second yield is reached whenever the first attempt raises URLError.
evidence.notes: Realistic exploitability depends on network position (MITM). Impact is integrity of metadata used for wheel selection.

flags.message: The unverified fallback is real and reachable. A URLError from the verified attempt, including a certificate verification failure under MITM, triggers the unverified retry, so an on-path attacker can serve forged PyPI JSON. Impact is limited to metadata used for version and upload-time selection, not the wheel payloads, which are fetched separately.
